slice: Hackers loot, Intel sinks, AI builds AI, watches nag, Vizag frets. Who minds the gate?

callouts.text: Stolen from Binance in the largest crypto heist yet, linked to North Korea.
Intel's worst day on record as cracks in the AI trade widened.

stories.title: North Korea-linked hackers steal $6.3bn from Binance in record heist
points: Hackers drained Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, on Thursday, taking $6.3bn by its own estimate within minutes. Researchers tie the attack to North Korea's state-backed TraderTraitor unit, also blamed for the earlier record Bybit heist.

Binance says the way in was an engineer's compromised laptop, though co-chief executive Richard Teng says the attack was more complex and more breach points have surfaced. Paused withdrawals revived memories of FTX online.

Tether and Circle froze stolen stablecoins fast, catching close to half the haul; the rest was swapped into coins nobody can freeze. Founder Changpeng Zhao says user funds are safe and losses will be covered.
stories.why: Crypto sells itself as money no one can seize, yet the only part of this loot that was recovered sat in coins a company could freeze. The heist tests both Binance's security pitch and the industry's case as a safe place to keep savings.
stories.other: Binance can absorb the loss and says customers are whole, and the record freeze shows the industry's response tools are getting faster. A rich, well-run state hacking unit may simply be beyond what any single firm can stop.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: $6.3bn stolen from Binance in minutes, linked to North Korean hackers; close to half frozen by stablecoin issuers.
stories.src: The Wall Street Journal and Financial Times
stories.emailTeaser: Hackers drained Binance; freezes saved close to half

stories.title: India saw 369 million cyber incidents in a year. Is it AI-ready?
points: Citing the Data Security Council of India, an ET commentary says 369 million security incidents were detected in 2024, about 702 a minute, with healthcare, hospitality and BFSI hit hardest. It flags a 42% shortage of skilled cyber staff and deepfakes used to beat KYC and money-laundering checks.

The writer calls for a national AI Act that fixes algorithmic liability, a stronger AI Safety Institute able to test models used in India, and company rules on AI use, noting a global study where 57% of employees hid their AI use at work.
stories.why: India's banking and identity systems run on digital checks that AI fakes can now fool. Without trained people and clear liability, more detection alone will not stop the losses.
stories.other: Part of the jump may reflect better detection rather than more attacks. And strict rules too early could slow AI uptake in a country that already ranks low on adoption.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: 369 million security incidents detected in India in 2024, about 702 a minute; the writer urges a national AI Act and stronger model testing.
stories.emailTeaser: 702 threats a minute and a 42% skills gap

stories.title: From Vizag to Thane, data centres meet local pushback
points: Villagers near Google's $15bn AI hub in Visakhapatnam allege land was taken back without proper consultation, and activists object to tree-clearing near the Kambalakonda sanctuary. In Thane, residents oppose Amazon's proposed 53-acre hyperscale site near homes, schools and hospitals.

An ET commentary says India needs the compute but should earn consent: water-saving cooling and clean power, siting away from cities where possible, visible benefits for host communities, and rules set before the damage. It suggests treating big data centres as quasi-public utilities.
stories.why: India's AI ambitions depend on building compute at home. If communities feel they carry the costs while others get the gains, protests could become the real bottleneck, not chips or money.
stories.other: Sites far from cities mean higher costs and slower service for some uses, and community payouts can slide into bribes for bad projects. Utility-style rules could also deter the investment India is courting.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: Google's $15bn Vizag AI hub and Amazon's Thane site face local pushback; the writer urges better tech, siting, community benefits and early rules.
stories.emailTeaser: Why data centres should run like public utilities

stories.title: Intel's record crash caps a week when the AI trade cracked
points: Intel fell 29% on Friday, its worst session ever, after warning that memory-chip prices inflated by the AI boom will keep PC sales weak, the WSJ reports. The Nasdaq composite fell 2.9%, its worst day since June.

Alphabet had its worst day on record as Google's search-ad growth slowed, partly due to AI mode, while Amazon's free cash flow plunged. With the Fed raising rates in September, heavy AI spending now reads as a burden.
An FT Unhedged column argues cash flow is what moves these stocks now: Meta, Alphabet and Amazon were punished for spending more than expected, while Microsoft's restraint kept its shares steadier.
stories.why: For months the biggest tech firms calmed AI doubts by printing profits. If their own earnings growth is now slowing, the trade loses the cushion that kept smaller, debt-laden AI players afloat, and index-heavy portfolios feel it first.
stories.other: One bad week is not a bust. Some investors expect AI listings and a calmer Middle East to restart the rally, and steep falls in quality names have often proved buying chances.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: Intel fell 29% in its worst day on record and the Nasdaq slid 2.9%; investors now reward cash flow over AI spending.
stories.src: The Wall Street Journal and Financial Times
stories.emailHead: The AI trade hits a wall
stories.emailTeaser: Intel drops 29% as Big Tech earnings disappoint

stories.title: How North Korea turned hacking into a state income machine
points: Cut off by sanctions, North Korea has built cyber warfare into a way to earn foreign currency, the FT reports. Students strong in maths and science are picked as teenagers and trained for years, some abroad in China and Russia.

Its record runs from the Sony Pictures hack and a Bangladesh central bank raid to crypto heists at Ronin, Bybit and now Binance. Blockchain firm Chainalysis says its hackers stole about $2bn last year, most of the world's total.
It also plants fake remote workers in foreign firms. Pyongyang denies all of it.
stories.why: Exchanges and banks are not up against freelance criminals but a state that recruits, trains and protects its hackers, and uses the loot to fund weapons. One expert warns AI will make such attacks faster to find and automate.
stories.other: Attribution rests on investigators and analysts, and Pyongyang calls it slander. Faster freezes and tracing may also shrink what each heist actually nets, so headline sums overstate the regime's take.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: North Korean hackers stole about $2bn last year, most of the world's crypto theft; the state trains hackers from their teens.
stories.emailTeaser: A state system that grooms coders to steal

stories.title: Apollo lends as OpenAI-backed Thrive buys ADT for $15bn
points: Thrive Holdings, spun out of Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital and backed by OpenAI, is buying home-alarm network ADT for $15bn including debt. Apollo, a past owner that made modest returns on it, is financing the deal.

The FT's Lex column says a new breed of AI-focused owners is promising bold makeovers of old businesses, while firms like Apollo shift from buyouts to corporate lending: steadier interest, less risk and less upside.
stories.why: It shows where private capital is heading: AI-driven owners chase the equity upside, while the old guard collects interest. For investors in buyout and private-credit funds, the returns mix is changing.
stories.other: An AI-led makeover of an alarm company is still a theory, and a buyer paying a big premium has less room for error. Lenders also lose if a heavily financed bet goes wrong.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: Thrive Holdings buys ADT for $15bn including debt, with Apollo lending; AI-focused buyers take equity while the old guard shifts to credit.
stories.emailTeaser: AI buyers take ADT; Apollo takes the interest

stories.title: AI now leads a quarter of AI research at Anthropic, company data show
points: A WSJ column spotlights an Anthropic chart tracking how much of its AI research is done by AI. The share where AI leads the work, with a human supervising, rose from 1% in March to 26% in August; none of it is yet fully autonomous.

The idea behind it is recursive self-improvement: each better model helps build a better one. Lab leaders call it vital to stay ahead and also a serious risk, and Anthropic itself says it is not inevitable but could arrive before institutions are ready.
Co-founder Jack Clark has pulled his own estimate for it forward to next year.
stories.why: If AI does most of the work on its own successors, progress could speed up beyond what companies, regulators and markets plan for. Who keeps oversight, and how, becomes a practical question rather than a science-fiction one.
stories.other: The numbers come from Anthropic's own AI rating its own work, on a company scale with no outside audit. Leading a task under supervision is not the same as independent invention, and a company heading for a listing has reasons to show fast progress.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: AI led 26% of AI research work at Anthropic in August, up from 1% in March; none is fully autonomous yet.
stories.emailHead: When AI builds the next AI
stories.emailTeaser: Claude led 26% of Anthropic's AI research by August

stories.title: Biomedical engineering is booming, but can health care keep up?
points: A Nature editorial says biomedical-engineering papers in the Nature Index grew 70% from 2021 to 2025, with China now well ahead of the US. Its worry: whether the surge reaches patients.

A Nature feature shows the strain. Smartwatches worn by hundreds of millions pour heart, sleep and stress data on doctors; one patient checked her watch's ECG 916 times in a year. Trials test watch alerts to take blood thinners only when needed, but false alarms put families off seizure alerts.
Nature also profiles researchers such as Xinyu Dong, who makes tough hydrogel e-skin, and James Eills, who sharpens MRI signals.
stories.why: The hard part of health tech is shifting from invention to absorption. Without standards and clear roles, clinics risk drowning in readings that no one has time to judge, and the promise of cheap, constant monitoring goes unused.
stories.other: A data flood is also an early-warning system: some patients already get diagnosed from watch alerts, and AI triage could sort the noise. Past lab advances such as hydrogels and MRI did become routine care; this wave may simply need time.

takeaway.line: Speed thrilled markets for years. This week it served thieves, spooked investors and left the neighbours of new data centres asking who signed off.
